name: Pakyong and the Silk Route
tagline: River valleys, caravan villages and the Zuluk loops
meta_description: Pakyong district and the Old Silk Route: Aritar, Zuluk, Nathang, Rongli permits, Indians-only rules, altitude and honest 2026 costs from Sikkim Escapes.
summary: Pakyong district, carved from East Sikkim in 2021, runs from the Teesta at Rangpo (about 330 m) to the Jelep La ridge above Kupup (about 4,000 m). It holds the Old Silk Route: Aritar's lake, Rongli's permit office, Zuluk's zigzag road and Nathang's yak meadows. The high road beyond Rongli is open to Indian nationals only.
intro: Pakyong district is the youngest corner of Sikkim on the map and one of the oldest on the trade routes. It was formed in December 2021 from the Pakyong, Rangpo and Rongli subdivisions of the old East Sikkim district, and covers about 404 square kilometres. The 2011 census counted about 74,600 people in that area. Its southern edge is the Rangpo river, which divides Sikkim from Kalimpong district of West Bengal; its eastern edge is the high ridge with Bhutan and Tibet.

Most travellers know the district by one name: the Silk Route. For centuries mule caravans carried wool and furs down from Tibet over Jelep La and climbed back with cloth, sugar and metal goods, by way of Kupup, Nathang, Zuluk, Rongli, Rhenock and Pedong to the wool market at Kalimpong. The trade ended after 1962, when the passes closed. The army road that replaced the mule path is now National Highway 717B, and its stacked hairpins above Zuluk are among the most photographed roads in the Himalaya.

Below the high road lies a quieter district that many people drive straight through. Aritar has a long lake, a dak bungalow built in 1895 and family homestays. Mankhim hill holds a temple of the Kirat Rai. Rolep, Lingtam and Padamchen are farming villages along the rivers, and Rhenock, Rorathang and Rangpo are market towns where large cardamom, ginger and broom grass change hands in season. Pakyong town, the headquarters, sits below Sikkim's only airport, which has had no scheduled flights since June 2024.

The district climbs from about 330 m at Rangpo to around 4,000 m near Kupup within roughly 100 km of road, so plan the altitude the way you would plan North Sikkim: one night low at Aritar, Rolep or Lingtam, then Padamchen or Zuluk, then Nathang. Beyond Rongli you need a Silk Route permit, and only Indian nationals may go. Foreign friends can share the lower villages with you. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: The wool road to Kalimpong and the 1888 campaign
story.text: The trade path through Pakyong district was once the busiest link between Tibet and British India. Wikipedia's article on Jelep La describes the Kalimpong route over the pass as the one that boosted local economies through the trade in wool and furs, passing Rongli, Rhenock, Pedong and Algarah. Its strategic value made it a battlefield. In 1886 Tibetan troops crossed Jelep La and built a fort and gate at Lingtu, on the ridge above Zuluk, about 21 km inside Sikkim. Britain sent an ultimatum to withdraw by 15 March 1888. In January that year, according to Wikipedia's account of the Sikkim expedition, the 32nd Pioneers were sent ahead to repair the Rongli bridge and the road. Brigadier-General Thomas Graham's column then marched up from Pedong, and a detachment of 200 men was posted at Pakyong. On 20 March Graham's men carried the Tibetan stockade at Jeluk, the old spelling of Zuluk, and the next day took the Lingtu fort. A larger Tibetan attack on the British camp at Gnathong, today's Nathang, was beaten off in May. The 1890 Convention of Calcutta then fixed the Sikkim–Tibet boundary. Trade flowed again, and John Claude White, Sikkim's first Political Officer, built a dak bungalow at Aritar in 1895. When you drive from Rongli up to Nathang, you follow the line of that campaign almost bend for bend.
story.source: Wikipedia: Jelep La; Wikipedia: Sikkim expedition; Wikipedia: Convention of Calcutta; Wikipedia: Aritar, Sikkim

little_known.fact: Pakyong's name is usually explained from the Lepcha pa yong, meaning bamboo of the bow, following the Lepcha habit of naming a place after something useful that grew there.
Pakyong Airport sits at about 1,416 m on a ridge built up with embankments, one of them around 263 ft high. It opened in 2018, but has had no scheduled flights since June 2024.
little_known.source: Wikipedia: Pakyong Airport; Sikkim Escapes facts memo

little_known.fact: The Rangpo river, Sikkim's third largest after the Teesta and Rangeet, rises at Menmecho Lake below Jelep La and runs past Rolep, Rongli and Rorathang to meet the Teesta at Rangpo.
little_known.source: Wikipedia: Rangpo River; Wikipedia: Lake Menmecho

little_known.fact: Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, set up in 2002 over about 124 km² between roughly 1,760 m and 4,390 m, has eco-development committees in Mankhim, Dalapchand, Lingtam, Padamchen, Zuluk and Gnathang.
Wikipedia records that Sikkim's first police outpost began work at Aritar in 1897, on the premises of the 1895 dak bungalow, where the state's first treasury was also set up.
little_known.source: Wikipedia: Aritar, Sikkim; Wikipedia: John Claude White

highlights.title: The Zuluk loops at sunrise
highlights.text: From Zuluk at about 2,800 m, a 30–40 minute pre-dawn drive takes you to Thambi View Point at about 3,400 m. On clear mornings from October to March the Kangchenjunga range lights up to the west and the hairpin road appears below you. Indian nationals only.

highlights.title: Nathang Valley and Kupup
highlights.text: A wide high valley at about 3,750 m with yak herders, a small gumpa and a memorial to the 1888 fighting at Gnathong. Above it, Kupup and the Jelep La ridge reach close to 4,000 m. Visit after a night at Zuluk, never on your first day.

highlights.title: Aritar and Lampokhari lake
highlights.text: A long natural lake at about 1,450 m with paddle boats, a lakeside path, an 1895 dak bungalow and a Kagyu gumpa. Aritar needs no special permit, so it is where mixed groups with foreign friends can stay together.

highlights.title: Mankhim hill and the Kirat Rai temple
highlights.text: A 30-minute drive above Aritar, at about 1,980 m, the Mangkhim temple of the Rai community looks out over the Rangpo valley. Sunrise views of the snow peaks on clear mornings, and the Sakewa festival dances in spring.

highlights.title: River villages: Rolep and Lingtam
highlights.text: Farming hamlets at about 1,200–1,400 m along the upper Rangpo river and the Rongli river, with family homestays, terraced fields and riverbank walks. The best first or last night of a Silk Route trip, and a slow trip of their own.

highlights.title: Padamchen forest and the Pangolakha sanctuary
highlights.text: Padamchen, at about 2,200 m, sits in the mixed forest of the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary. Spring rhododendrons, laughingthrushes and minlas at dawn, and a gentle acclimatisation night before Zuluk and Nathang.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP). Pakyong Airport has had no scheduled flights since June 2024. From NJP the usual road follows NH10 up the Teesta to Rangpo, about 90 km and 3–3.5 hours, then climbs via Rorathang to Rongli, about 110 km and 4–4.5 hours in all. NH10 closes after monsoon slides; the alternative is via Kalimpong, Pedong and Reshi into Rhenock, which follows the old trade road. From Gangtok, Rongli is about 65 km and 2.5–3 hours via Ranipool, Pakyong and Rorathang. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok and Siliguri to Rongli, Rhenock and Rangpo. Beyond Rongli you need a permit-registered vehicle. The Sevoke–Rangpo railway is not open yet; completion is targeted for December 2027. Check current status before you travel.
permits: The upper Silk Route beyond Rongli, including Lingtam, Padamchen, Zuluk, Thambi View Point, Nathang and Kupup, is a protected area open to Indian nationals only. The permit is processed at Rongli for named people, dates and a vehicle, usually through a registered agent, driver or homestay; carry original photo ID, copies and two passport photos. Foreign nationals, including OCI holders, are not allowed beyond Rongli, but Aritar, Mankhim, Rhenock, Rorathang, Rangpo and Pakyong town need only the general Sikkim entry permit. For Rolep, ask us. Check current status before you travel.
money: On a budget, two people sharing a reserved car from NJP for a 3-night Silk Route loop with homestays and meals should plan on about ₹9,000–12,000 each, including permits. Homestays across the district run at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with dinner and breakfast, and a shared jeep seat from Gangtok to Rongli costs about ₹200–300. A value trip with a private SUV and the better Aritar and Padamchen houses comes to about ₹20,000–28,000 per person for 5 nights. Comfort travellers can add nights at Vivanta Sikkim in Pakyong, at about ₹9,000–16,000 a room. All prices are indicative.

months.weather: Zuluk −6 to 6 °C, snow likely; Aritar 4 to 15 °C
months.summary: The coldest month. Zuluk, Thambi and Nathang often lie under snow, which makes the loops beautiful and the road unreliable: closures of a day or more are common. The lower villages are dry, clear and cool, with frosty mornings at Aritar and sharp views of the snow peaks from Mankhim. Mid-January brings Maghe Sankranti, when families gather at the rivers at Rangpo. Keep spare days if you want snow, and check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Book homestays with extra quilts and carry thermals, gloves and a warm cap for everyone.

months.weather: Zuluk −4 to 8 °C, snow possible; Aritar 6 to 17 °C
months.summary: Still winter up high, with snow possible at Zuluk and Nathang and the Kupup road often closed after heavy falls. Lower down the days warm up, and the first rhododendrons begin to show in the forests around Padamchen late in the month. Losar, the Tibetan new year, usually falls in February or early March; Aritar Gumpa marks it with prayers and butter lamps. Quiet roads and low prices make it a good month for flexible travellers.
months.tip: Plan the high night for the end of the trip so a snow closure only shortens it, not ends it.

months.summary: Spring arrives. Rhododendrons flower from the Padamchen forests upwards as the month goes on, the snow line retreats, and the high road usually becomes reliable again. Mornings can still be clear enough for Kangchenjunga from Thambi. Lampokhari and the Aritar fields turn green, and the lower villages are warm by midday. Afternoon thunderstorms start to appear late in the month, so do your viewpoints early. Losar sometimes falls in early March.
months.tip: Leave for Thambi in the dark: by 9 am spring haze often hides the peaks.

months.summary: Rhododendron month on the Silk Route. Red, pink and white blooms climb from about 2,200 m at Padamchen to above Zuluk and Thambi, and birds are active in the Pangolakha forests. Haze softens the mountain views, but days are mild everywhere. From the Baisakh full moon, usually in late April or May, the Rai community gathers on Mankhim hill for Sakewa. Weekends get busy with families from Bengal, so book Zuluk early.
months.tip: Ask your homestay to arrange a dawn forest walk around Padamchen for birds and flowers.

months.summary: Warm, green and busy. Rhododendrons linger at the higher end of the route early in the month, the Nathang meadows start to green up, and the lower villages are good for river walks at Rolep. Pre-monsoon storms bring afternoon rain and the first slides by late May. Sakewa celebrations at Mankhim often fall in May. School holidays fill Aritar and Zuluk, so plan rooms well ahead.
months.tip: Start road days early, as afternoon storms and fog are common by the end of the month.

months.weather: Zuluk 9 to 17 °C, heavy rain; Rongli 20 to 30 °C
months.summary: The monsoon arrives around the second week of June. Rain is heavy, fog sits on the loops, and slides cut NH10 and the Rongli–Zuluk road often, sometimes for days. Views of the snow peaks are rare. The lower villages are lush and quiet, and Aritar and Rolep still work for a slow stay if you keep dates flexible. We do not suggest the high Silk Route this month. Check current status before you travel.
months.tip: If you must travel, choose the Kalimpong–Pedong–Rhenock road when NH10 is shut.

months.weather: Zuluk 10 to 17 °C, very wet; Aritar 17 to 25 °C
months.summary: The wettest stretch of the year. Expect rain most days, leeches on forest paths and frequent road cuts. The Rangpo river runs high and fast, so stay well away from the water at Rolep and Rangpo. The high road is sometimes open between slides, but the views are usually lost in cloud. Lower-village homestays offer discounts to the few travellers who come. Check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Pack leech socks and a good rain jacket if you plan any walks.

months.summary: Still monsoon, with heavy rain and slides on most roads. Green paddy terraces at Aritar and Lingtam are at their brightest, and waterfalls on the Rorathang–Rongli road are full. Large cardamom harvest begins in some villages towards the end of the month. The Silk Route is possible on lucky days but not something to plan a holiday around. Check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Book refundable stays and keep the last day free in case a slide holds you up.

months.summary: The rains ease through the month, though heavy showers and slides still happen in the first half. By late September the air clears, the first sharp mountain mornings return and roads are repaired. It is a quiet, good-value time for the lower villages and, late in the month, for the high road. Cardamom drying is under way in the farming villages. Check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Aim for the last ten days of the month for the best balance of clear skies and low prices.

months.summary: The best month for views. Clear, cold mornings show the Kangchenjunga range from Thambi, Lungthung and Mankhim, and the Nathang grass begins to turn gold. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays bring crowds and higher rates, especially at Zuluk and Aritar. Permit queues at Rongli can be long on Saturdays. Book rooms and cars a month or more ahead.
months.tip: Send ID scans two days ahead so your permit is ready at Rongli.

months.summary: Clear, dry and cold, with the most reliable mountain views of the year and fewer crowds than October. Nathang is golden and frosty, the paddy at Aritar is harvested, and night temperatures at Zuluk fall below freezing. In late autumn the Rai community holds the Udhauli gathering of Sakewa at Mankhim in some years. A fine month for photographers and families with warm clothes.
months.tip: Pack a down or padded jacket: dawn at Thambi is well below zero.

months.weather: Zuluk −4 to 8 °C, first snow likely; Aritar 6 to 17 °C
months.summary: Early winter. The first snow usually reaches Zuluk and Nathang in late December, and clear days give long views. Roads can close after a heavy fall, so build in a spare day. The Christmas–New Year week fills Aritar and Zuluk with families from Kolkata and Siliguri. The lower villages stay mild and sunny, ideal for walks around Lampokhari and the Rhenock bazaar.
months.tip: Book the Christmas week by October, and keep the high night flexible in case of snow.

faqs.q: Is Pakyong district the same as the Old Silk Route?
faqs.a: Mostly. The district includes the Sikkim stretch of the old Kalimpong–Tibet trade road, from Rhenock and Rongli up through Zuluk and Nathang towards Jelep La. Kupup itself falls in Gangtok district. Pakyong district also covers Pakyong town, Rangpo, Rorathang and quiet villages like Aritar and Rolep that most Silk Route trips pass through.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit the Silk Route?
faqs.a: No. Foreign nationals, including OCI holders, are not allowed beyond Rongli, so Zuluk, Thambi View Point, Nathang and Kupup are closed to them. They can stay at Aritar, Mankhim, Rhenock and Pakyong town with the general Sikkim entry permit applied for online on the e-FRRO portal. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there flights to Pakyong Airport?
faqs.a: Not at present. Pakyong Airport has had no scheduled flights since June 2024. Plan your trip on Bagdogra (IXB), about 115–125 km and 4.5–5 hours from Rongli, or New Jalpaiguri (NJP) railway station, about 110 km and 4–4.5 hours. If flights resume we will update this page, but check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Pakyong and the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Three nights is the minimum for a loop from Gangtok to Zuluk and Nathang. We prefer four or five nights from NJP or Bagdogra: Aritar or Lingtam first, then Padamchen or Zuluk, then Nathang or a second Zuluk night, and back via Rongli or, when open, via Kupup and Tsomgo to Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Silk Route?
faqs.a: October to December for clear mountain views, and March to May for rhododendrons. January and February bring snow but frequent road closures. Avoid mid-June to mid-September, when monsoon slides cut NH10 and the Rongli–Zuluk road and clouds hide the peaks. The lower villages such as Aritar are pleasant all year. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a problem on the Silk Route?
faqs.a: It can be, because the road climbs from about 830 m at Rongli to about 3,750 m at Nathang in a few hours. Sleep the first night low at Aritar, Lingtam or Rolep, then Padamchen or Zuluk, and only then go to Nathang. Drink water, avoid alcohol on the first high night, and descend if headaches worsen.

faqs.q: Where do I get the Silk Route permit?
faqs.a: At Rongli, the subdivision town at the foot of the high road. Your driver, agent or homestay usually files it from scans of your photo ID, and you collect it on the way up. Carry originals, photocopies and two passport photos. The government fee is about ₹200 per person, plus handling. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we do the Silk Route by shared jeep?
faqs.a: Only part of it. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok and Siliguri to Rongli and Rhenock for about ₹200–400 a seat. Above Rongli, local jeeps serve residents once or twice a day, and above Zuluk there is no shared transport. In practice you need a reserved, permit-registered car for the high road, which a group can share.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATMs in Pakyong district?
faqs.a: Pakyong, Rangpo, Rorathang, Rhenock and Rongli have ATMs and decent mobile coverage. Above Rongli there are no ATMs, and signal is patchy at Zuluk and weak at Nathang. Withdraw cash at Rhenock or Rongli, download offline maps, and tell your family you may be out of touch for a night.
